KEY MESSAGE 1...
Summer certainly stuck around one more day with 5/6 regional 
climate sites striking high temperatures in the low to mid 80s. 
Our high water mark was at PHD, where an afternoon high of 85 
degrees broke the previous record high for today (81 degrees in 
1995). Nocturnal cooling will be hard to come by tonight with 
elevated wind, high dew points, and increasing cloud cover 
holding overnight lows in the low to mid 60s. An areal record 
high was set, but record warm lows on Wednesday are less likely 
with cooler temperatures Wednesday night.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
A slow moving cold front finally gets a kick and moves through our 
area north to south on Wednesday returning showers and a few storms. 
Some storms could get a bit on the stronger side, but the primary 
limiting factor to that will be a displaced instability axis 
from the highest shear. The belt of strongest mid-level flow, 
and thus deep layer shear, will be to our north. The best 
opportunity for heating and better instability will be off to 
our south in the thinner cloud cover out ahead of the front. 
REFS joint probability for >500 J/kg of SBCAPE and >30 knots of 
shear peaks south of I-70 into northern WV around 60-90% with a 
sharp cutoff north owing to much less destabilization. So, the 
area to watch for storms to get more feisty and bring a low-end 
damaging wind threat would be to the south, confident with 
SPC's Marginal Risk. Can't entirely rule out some localized 
higher rainfall totals in northern WV where REFS prob for 
>1"/hour reaches around 40%, but this will be highly dependent 
on training with east-west motion and any impacts would only be 
in the urban areas.

KEY MESSAGE 3...
The most impactful system arrives on Friday ushering in strong wind 
gusts, well below normal temperatures, and showers. While some 
uncertainty remains among ensembles primarily owing to timing and, 
to a lesser extent, depth of the mid-level trough, confidence in all 
three impacts remains high. Deep surface low pressure will pull a 
cold front through the area on Friday with a tight pressure 
gradient, 10+ dam 500 mb height falls in 12 hours, and strong low-
level cold advection.

For the wind threat, the combination of the tight gradient and 
mixing into a 40-45 knot low level jet should result in widespread 
gusts of 35-45 mph. They'll be stronger across our higher elevation 
where probability for Wind Advisory criteria gusts >46 mph reaches 
up to ~60%. Eastern Tucker County runs an elevated probability for 
High Wind Warning criteria gusts >58 mph also up to around 60%. 
Current NBM probability for Advisory criteria gusts in the lower 
elevation is around 30-40%, so certainly can't be ruled out, but 
headlines look most likely in the ridges.

Strong cold advection in post-frontal northwest flow will bottom out 
ensemble mean 850 mb temperatures to around -2 to -4C. An 
unseasonably cold air mass will settle in for the first half of
the weekend providing the potential for two nights of frost and
freeze. Friday night, probabilities are a bit less bullish 
outside of our I-80 counties where 30-40% sneaks in for <32F, 
but frost concerns could be higher with probability for <36F 
reaching 70-80% north of Pittsburgh and down the ridges. 
Saturday daytime highs will feel more like those of mid to late 
November only warming to near 50 degrees with 40s in the 
elevation. The gradient will relax some Sunday night allowing 
wind to slacken and skies will clear. This could point toward 
Saturday night being the coldest areawide with better 
radiational cooling conditions amid a dry, cold airmass. The dew
point could be the floor for lows with optimal radiation, and 
this suggests widespread low to mid 30s and upper 20s. A 
widespread frost is likely. Probability for a freeze ranges from
40-80% in eastern OH, northern WV, and western PA, with the 
highest values away from urban areas and in the higher 
elevation. Expect that we'll be looking at some combination of 
frost/freeze headlines on top of wind headlines in the next 
couple days.

Two rounds of precip are possible both along the front itself and 
then in the wrap around cold advection across the lakes on Saturday. 
Strong flow amid the dynamic system could drive some "power showers" 
accompanying FROPA on Friday bringing enhanced gusts with them 
provided they're able to get tall enough to tap into the 40-50 knots 
a few thousand feet off the ground. We'll have to see what the 
thermodynamic profile looks like as the CAMs come into play in the 
next 24-36 hours, but the current RRFS does show enough fumes of 
SBCAPE. Then, continued cold advection in northwest flow likely 
results in some lake effect and upslope precip late Friday into 
early Saturday. For most, this will be a cool, windy scattered 
rain/graupel shower setup. For some, the first novelty snowflakes of
